text:
This case is about a tragic death from terminal metastatic melanoma, not a State-caused deprivation of life. The contemporaneous medical file, radiology from 24–29 September 2009, and the 16 October autopsy all show rapidly progressive brain and systemic metastases, neurological decline, respiratory failure on 6 October, and death on 15 October from malignant melanoma with multiple brain metastases, cerebral haemorrhage, and cerebral oedema—not from restraint, medication, starvation, or withdrawal of ventilation. Under Article 2, Estonia’s obligation is to provide an adequate legal and medical framework and an effective investigation, not to guarantee recovery where curative treatment had become futile; here, the hospital repeatedly reassessed O., the medical council moved to palliative care on 28 September and 6 October for documented clinical reasons, and the later forensic report of 30 August 2012 confirmed that the medicines were appropriate, feeding was discontinued only after findings corresponding to brain death while infusion therapy continued, and mechanical ventilation was stopped only after cardiac arrest on 15 October. The applicant’s theory of overdose, improper restraint, and premature ending of life is contradicted by the records themselves, by witness statements from doctors, nurses, and visitors, and by the pathology evidence.
[Law-library check: Article 2 (verified)]

This case is not about whether O. was terminally ill; it is about whether Estonia discharged its Article 2 duty to protect life when life-ending decisions were taken on 13–15 October 2009 without a reliably documented brain-death process and without an effective response to the mother’s immediate complaint. The NEMC chart extracts show critical gaps exactly where the State says certainty existed: a brain-death verification sheet is unsigned, the time for repeat confirmation is blank, and there is no separate signed record that the family was informed when feeding was stopped; an independent anaesthesiologist later confirmed that the records do not clearly document the legal-medical sequence and are too sparse on sedation and neurological status to exclude masking of clinical signs. The applicant also immediately alleged on 15 October that treatment had been stopped before death and expressly asked police for an expert examination, yet her call was logged merely as an “information notice,” delaying a proper criminal-law response. Under Article 2, where a patient dies after disputed withdrawal of sustaining treatment, the State must ensure both a clear protective medical framework and an effective investigation; here, the documentation failures, the premature cessation of nutrition, and the superficiality concerns surrounding the Expert Committee review show those obligations were not met.
[Law-library check: Article 2 (verified)]

The 30 August 2012 Estonian Forensic Science Institute report answering the prosecutor's ten questions, concluding that the medications administered were appropriate and did not stop O.'s breathing, that restraints could be justified in his disturbed condition, that discontinuation of feeding after findings corresponding to brain death while continuing infusion therapy was medically justified, and that ventilation was turned off only after the heart had stopped.

NEMC nursing chart extracts for 13-14 October 2009, obtained by the applicant from the hospital file, showing that after the notation of findings corresponding to brain death there is no fully completed brain-death verification protocol in the chart: one neurological assessment sheet is unsigned, the time for a repeat confirmation is left blank, and no separate signed record of informing the family about cessation of feeding appears in the file.

Under Article 2 § 1 of the Convention, the question is not whether every step in a terminal patient’s chart was perfectly documented, but whether the State unlawfully deprived O. of life or failed in its positive obligations to protect life through an adequate medical and investigative response. On these facts, the objective medical evidence is consistent and one-directional: the radiology of 24–29 September showed leptomeningeal and widespread metastatic spread; the ICU file records progressive respiratory failure on 6 October, pneumonia treatment, continued infusion therapy after 13 October, and ventilation being discontinued only after cardiac arrest on 15 October; and the autopsy and death certificate identify malignant melanoma with multiple brain metastases, cerebral haemorrhage and cerebral oedema as the cause of death, with no finding of death by restraint, medication overdose, starvation, or withdrawal of ventilation. The applicant’s strongest point is an incomplete brain-death form, but Article 2 § 1 is not violated by a paperwork irregularity where the substantive evidence shows that O. was terminal, received palliative and supportive care, and was not killed by any act or omission of the hospital; nor is there an Article 2 procedural failure where the State obtained the full medical file, witness statements, autopsy materials, and a forensic report answering ten specific causation questions before the prosecutor discontinued the case.
[Law-library check: Article 2 § 1 of the Convention (verified); Article 2 § 1 (verified); Article 2 (verified)]

Article 2 § 1 of the Convention protects not only against intentional killing but requires the State to put in place and operate an effective framework when medical decisions foreseeably end life; that duty is especially acute where sustaining treatment is withdrawn on the basis of brain death. Here, the State’s own justification for stopping feeding on 13 October depends on a valid brain-death determination, yet the hospital chart for 13–14 October contains an unsigned neurological assessment, a blank time for repeat confirmation, and no signed record that the family was informed of the cessation of feeding; those are not harmless clerical slips but defects going to whether the life-ending decision was lawfully and reliably taken at all. The procedural limb of Article 2 is also engaged: on 15 October the applicant expressly asked police for an expert examination and alleged treatment had been stopped before death, but the matter was logged only as an 'information notice', showing that the State’s immediate response to a credible life-related complaint was inadequate rather than prompt and effective.
[Law-library check: Article 2 § 1 of the Convention (verified); Article 2 (verified)]

Autopsy report and preserved pathology materials from the NEMC pathology centre, together with the medical death certificate, identifying malignant melanoma with multiple brain metastases, cerebral haemorrhage and cerebral oedema as the fatal process, with no finding consistent with death caused by restraint, withdrawal of ventilation, or an acute toxic medication event.

Telephone log information from the emergency call of 15 October 2009 and the applicant's follow-up written complaint to police, showing that she expressly asked for an expert examination and alleged that treatment had been stopped before death, while the matter was registered only as an information notice rather than as a crime report at that stage.

Article 2 § 1 of the Convention does not turn every disputed medical record into a right-to-life violation; the applicant must show that the State caused or failed to prevent a deprivation of life, or failed to provide an effective framework and investigation. Here, even taking the 13–14 October documentation criticism at its highest, the decisive causation evidence is unchanged: the full hospital course showed progressive respiratory failure from 6 October, antibacterial treatment for pneumonia, continued infusion therapy after 13 October, and mechanical ventilation discontinued only after cardiac arrest on 15 October; the autopsy and forensic report both identified metastatic melanoma with cerebral haemorrhage and oedema as the cause of death and excluded medication, restraint, starvation, or withdrawal of ventilation as the cause. As to the procedural limb of Article 2, the State did investigate effectively: after the 15 October complaint, authorities obtained the medical file, autopsy materials, witness statements from doctors, nurses and visitors, and a forensic report answering ten targeted questions before terminating the case on 25 October 2012. The plaintiff’s strongest point is an incomplete brain-death form, but Article 2 § 1 is not violated by an imperfect form where the substantive medical and forensic record consistently shows that O. died from terminal metastatic disease, not from any unlawful act or omission by the hospital or the State.
[Law-library check: Article 2 § 1 of the Convention (verified); Article 2 (verified); Article 2 § 1 (verified)]

The defendant’s strongest point is the autopsy and 2012 forensic report, but neither cures the critical Article 2 defect: they explain why O. was dying, not whether the State lawfully and reliably determined brain death before stopping feeding on 13 October. The hospital’s own chart is missing a completed verification sequence, and the independent anaesthesiologist’s opinion based on that file states that the records do not clearly document the legal-medical sequence for diagnosing brain death and are too sparse on sedation and neurological status on 12–13 October to exclude masking of clinical signs; that directly undercuts the later forensic conclusion, which depended on the same incomplete records. So this is not 'mere paperwork': when life-sustaining care is withdrawn because a patient is said to be brain-dead, unsigned assessments, a blank repeat-confirmation time, and sparse sedation charting go to the reliability of the life-ending decision itself.
[Law-library check: Article 2 (verified)]

Complete NEMC medical file, including ICU progress notes, medication charts, ventilator records and council entries, showing progressive metastatic disease with neurological decline, documented respiratory failure on 6 October 2009, antibacterial treatment for pneumonia, continued infusion therapy after 13 October 2009, and mechanical ventilation being discontinued only after cardiac arrest on 15 October 2009.

A written opinion obtained by the applicant from an independent anaesthesiologist after the Expert Committee proceedings, based on copies of the medical file, stating that the records do not clearly document the legal-medical sequence for diagnosing brain death, that cessation of nutrition should have been documented with greater precision, and that the charting of sedation and neurological status on 12-13 October 2009 is too sparse to exclude masking of clinical signs.

The applicant’s strongest remaining point is the independent anaesthesiologist’s criticism that the 12–13 October charting was too sparse to exclude masking of clinical signs, but that opinion does not establish an Article 2 violation because it is only a critique of record-keeping based on copies of the same file, not evidence that O. was alive in any legally meaningful sense or that treatment caused his death. Against that, the objective evidence is direct and consistent: the radiology of 24–29 September showed leptomeningeal and widespread metastatic spread; the full ICU record documents progressive respiratory failure from 6 October, pneumonia treatment, and continued infusion therapy after 13 October; the 16 October autopsy found death from malignant melanoma with multiple brain metastases, cerebral haemorrhage and cerebral oedema; and the 30 August 2012 forensic report expressly concluded that the medicines did not stop his breathing and that ventilation was turned off only after cardiac arrest on 15 October. So even if one accepts imperfect documentation of the brain-death sequence, the plaintiff still cannot bridge the essential causation gap under Article 2: there is no evidence that any omission by the hospital deprived O. of life, as opposed to his terminal metastatic disease doing so.
[Law-library check: Article 2 (verified)]

Article 2 § 1 of the Convention required Estonia not only to avoid directly causing death, but to operate a practical framework capable of protecting life at the moment when treatment was limited on 13 October 2009. On these facts, the State cannot rely on later autopsy findings about the underlying melanoma to answer the critical Article 2 question: whether the decision to stop feeding after findings 'corresponding to brain death' was taken through a reliable and properly documented process, when the hospital file itself contains an unsigned neurological assessment, a blank repeat-confirmation time, and sparse sedation/neurological charting that the independent anaesthesiologist said could not exclude masking of clinical signs. The procedural limb of Article 2 is also engaged because, after the applicant’s 15 October 2009 emergency call expressly alleging that treatment had been stopped before death and requesting an expert examination, the complaint was initially logged only as an information notice rather than treated with the immediacy a credible life-related complaint required; taken together, those substantive and procedural defects are sufficient to find a violation of Article 2 § 1 of the Convention.
[Law-library check: Article 2 § 1 of the Convention (verified); Article 2 (verified)]

Witness interview records from the criminal investigation, including statements from treating doctors, ICU nurses and visiting friends, indicating that O. was increasingly confused and at risk of self-harm before restraints were used, that staff continued monitoring and comfort care after active treatment ceased, and that visitors were told his condition was terminal and rapidly worsening.

Minutes and attendance data from the Expert Committee meeting of 25 March 2010, relied on by the applicant, indicating that some members who signed off on the decision did not personally question her at the hearing and that one of the outside opinions had been circulated in summary form only, which she uses to challenge the depth and impartiality of that review.

Under Article 2 § 1, the applicant must show that the State caused or failed to prevent a deprivation of life; she has not, because every objective source points the same way: the CT/MRI studies of 24–29 September 2009 showed leptomeningeal involvement of cranial nerves and probable widespread metastases to the liver and abdominal organs, the medical council on 28 September and again on 6 October concluded curative treatment was futile, and the complete ICU file records progressive respiratory failure on 6 October, pneumonia treatment, continued infusion therapy after 13 October, and mechanical ventilation being discontinued only after cardiac arrest on 15 October. The autopsy of 16 October and preserved pathology materials identify the fatal process as malignant melanoma with multiple brain metastases, cerebral haemorrhage and cerebral oedema, and the 30 August 2012 forensic report expressly answers the causation questions the applicant raises: the medicines did not stop his breathing, restraints were medically justifiable in his disturbed condition, feeding was stopped only after findings corresponding to brain death while infusion continued, and ventilation was turned off only after death.  

The plaintiff’s best point is the incomplete brain-death paperwork, but Article 2 is not violated by an unsigned or incomplete form where the substantive medical, radiological, pathological and witness evidence all show that O. was dying from overwhelming metastatic disease and was not killed by starvation, overdose, restraint, or withdrawal of ventilation. Nor is there a procedural violation: the authorities gathered the full file, radiology, autopsy materials, pathology, and witness statements from doctors, nurses and visitors, and obtained a forensic report addressing ten specific questions before ending the criminal case. On these facts, Estonia provided both care and investigation within its margin of appreciation, so the Article 2 claim should be denied.
[Law-library check: Article 2 § 1 (verified); Article 2 (verified)]

Article 2 required Estonia to operate a reliable life-protective framework at the very moment life-sustaining care was limited, and on 13–15 October 2009 that framework failed: the NEMC file has no fully completed brain-death verification protocol, one neurological assessment is unsigned, the repeat-confirmation time is blank, and there is no signed record that the family was informed when feeding was stopped. That is not cured by later autopsy findings about metastatic melanoma, because the issue is not whether O. was gravely ill, but whether the State lawfully and safely treated him as brain-dead before ceasing nutrition; the independent anaesthesiologist said the sedation and neurological charting on 12–13 October was too sparse to exclude masking of clinical signs, and the applicant’s bedside note from 14 October records that O.’s pulse rose when she spoke to him, while a relative confirmed the room window was ajar and he was only lightly covered. The State’s procedural response was also deficient under Article 2: on 15 October the applicant expressly asked police for an expert examination and alleged treatment had been stopped before death, yet the matter was logged merely as an information notice, and the later Expert Committee review was open to serious doubt because some signatories did not personally question her and one outside opinion was circulated only in summary form. The defendant’s best point—the autopsy and 2012 forensic report—shows only the underlying terminal disease; it does not repair the contemporaneous failures in the brain-death process or the State’s initial failure to react promptly and effectively to a credible life-related complaint, so the Court should find a violation of Article 2 § 1.
[Law-library check: Article 2 (verified); Article 2 § 1 (verified)]

variables.cause: Alleged violation of Article 2 § 1 (right to life)
variables.facts:
6. The applicant was born in 1963 and lives in Tallinn.
7. In 2006 the applicant’s son O., who was born in 1983, was diagnosed with malignant melanoma. He was operated on in 2006, and underwent regular check-ups. In April 2009 a metastasis was removed from his brain, and he received radiation therapy.
8. In September 2009 O.’s state of health deteriorated. He was vomiting and felt weak and dizzy.
9. On 19 September 2009 the applicant called an ambulance and O. was taken to the North Estonia Medical Centre (“the NEMC”) (Põhja-Eesti Regionaalhaigla) for examination. A computerised tomography (CT) scan was performed on him. According to the applicant, O. was told that the scan had not revealed any problems with his health. He was prescribed an anti-vomiting drug and discharged from the hospital the same evening.
10. On 24 September 2009 the applicant again called an ambulance for O., who had been complaining of feeling generally unwell, of a numbness of one side of his face, a rash around his nose and dizziness. O. was admitted to the NEMC. A CT scan and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of O.’s brain were performed the same day and the following day, respectively. An additional CT scan of O.’s neck, lungs, abdomen and pelvic area was performed on 29 September 2009. The MRI scan and the CT scan of 29 September 2009, taken together, indicated a leptomeningeal pathological process involving the cranial nerves, a probable meningeal metastatic process and probable multiple metastases in the liver and other organs of the abdominal cavity. He was given hormonal and infusion therapy, but his health deteriorated rapidly. He developed breathing and walking problems and a speech impediment, and his eyesight worsened. On 28 September 2009 a hospital medical council decided to proceed with palliative care. It found that because of the spread of the tumour, oncological treatment would not be effective. The applicant pointed out that the medical council’s decision had not been signed by O.
11. For one week starting from 5 October 2009, O. was physically restrained to a bed with magnetically locking restraints on both arms, apparently in order to prevent him from hurting himself, given his disturbed state of mind.
12. On 6 October 2009 O. was transferred to an intensive care unit because he was suffering from progressive respiratory failure and a disturbed state of mind. He was also diagnosed with pneumonia and, in the light of that finding, was given additional antibacterial treatment. According to the medical record (nurse’s notes), on 6 October 2009 O. was intubated because he was having breathing difficulties. On the same day the medical council found that a surgical cure would not be possible and decided to continue with palliative treatment supporting the vital functions. The applicant again pointed out that the medical council’s decision was not signed by O.
13. On 9 October 2009 a tracheotomy was performed on O.
14. On 12 October 2009 O. stopped breathing and mechanical ventilation was applied. On 13 October 2009 characteristics corresponding to brain death were ascertained. According to information in a report drawn up by the Estonian Forensic Science Institute based on an analysis of O.’s medical records, an electroencephalogram performed the same day revealed serious diffuse brain damage and only minimal electrical activity. O.’s active treatment and feeding were discontinued, but the infusion therapy was continued. The applicant disagreed with this finding and rather considered that O. had fallen into a coma following an overdose of medicine. She maintained that O.’s pulse had reacted to her speech the following day, 14 October 2009, which had indicated that O. had not been brain-dead. According to the applicant, the protocol for verifying brain death was never fully and properly carried out. The administration of food and medicines was not resumed, despite the applicant’s requests. The applicant alleged that during the night of 14 October 2009, O.’s blanket had been removed and he had been left with only a sheet near an open window, which had caused his body temperature to drop to 35 degrees Celsius.
15. On 15 October 2009 O.’s heart stopped and the mechanical ventilation was terminated.
16. On 15 October 2009 the applicant called the police on the general emergency number, complained about O.’s treatment and asked that an expert examination be commissioned. Her phone call was registered as an information notice (infoteade) and not as the reporting of a crime. The applicant was advised to contact the Expert Committee on the Quality of Health Care Services (Tervishoiuteenuse kvaliteedi ekspertkomisjon; hereinafter “the Expert Committee”).
17. On 16 October 2009 an autopsy was performed at the NEMC. The medical death certificate (arstlik surmateatis) indicated cerebral oedema as the immediate cause of death, and melanoma with multiple metastases as the medical condition that had brought about the immediate cause of death. According to the autopsy report (lahangu protokoll), O. died of malignant melanoma with multiple metastases in the brain, which also caused cerebral haemorrhage and oedema as complications.
18. On 2 November 2009 the applicant complained to the Health Board (Terviseamet) of O.’s inhuman treatment and about the circumstances of his death.
19. On 8 March 2010 the Health Board informed the applicant that the case had been transmitted to the Expert Committee. The Expert Committee examined O.’s medical records, obtained written explanations from several members of the medical staff who had treated O., and ordered two expert opinions, one to be prepared by one of its members and the other by another doctor, both professors emeriti. The Expert Committee also heard the applicant. In its decision given on 25 March 2010, it found no medical malpractice in O.’s treatment. According to the report of the Expert Committee’s meeting of 25 March 2010 at which the applicant was also present, the Expert Committee gave oral answers to the applicant’s questions regarding the possible radiation of O. during his previous treatment; the decision not to offer chemotherapy to O.; and the alleged late detection of pneumonia. In addition, the Expert Committee’s decision contained written answers to the applicant, stating that O. had not suffered from a stroke; that the deterioration in his health had not been caused by the administration of specific medication or the withdrawal thereof, but rather by the metastatic developments in his brain; and that based on the medical records, O. had not been starved, nor had his mechanical ventilation been stopped before his death. The applicant was also notified of the possibility to request an alternative medical expert opinion and was informed that tissue samples gathered while the patient was alive as well as after his death, would be maintained for thirty years at the NEMC pathology centre and were available on demand. The applicant considered that the Expert Committee had not been impartial, that it had lacked a quorum at its meeting of 25 March 2010 and that the decision it had adopted contained false statements. An action lodged by the applicant to have the Expert Committee’s report declared unlawful and claiming damages for it was dismissed by a final judgment of the Supreme Court on 2 December 2015.
20. In the meantime, on 22 March 2010 the applicant lodged an offence report with a prosecutor’s office. Criminal proceedings under Article 123 of the Penal Code (placing or leaving another person in a situation which is life-threatening or likely to cause serious damage to the person’s health) were initiated on 1 April 2010.
21. In the course of the criminal investigation, several individuals (doctors, nurses, the applicant, and O.’s friends who had visited him in the hospital) were interviewed. Requests for documentary evidence (the Expert Committee’s opinion, O.’s medical file as well as the autopsy report) were submitted and documents were received; a forensic medical examination was ordered from the Estonian Forensic Science Institute. The prosecutor posed ten questions to the forensic medical experts addressing, inter alia, O.’s diagnoses; the adequacy of the treatment with respect to his state of health (including the tracheotomy); the restraining of O. to the bed; the administration of medicine on 12 October 2009 and whether this could have caused O.’s breathing to stop; the decision to cease the administration of medicine and food on 13 October 2009; the assertion that O. was brain-dead; and the decision to stop mechanical ventilation.
22. According to the forensic medical report dated 30 August 2012, O. had received treatment appropriate for his condition. The forensic medical experts also concluded that the medicine administered to O. had been appropriate and had not caused his breathing to stop. They considered that the restraining of O. to the bed could have been justified in the instant case. As the characteristics corresponding to brain death had been ascertained, the discontinuation of feeding and the continuation of infusion therapy had been medically justified. The experts also concluded that the mechanical ventilation had been turned off only after his heart had stopped and thus could not have been the cause of his death. The forensic medical assessment found that O.’s death had been caused by malignant melanoma with multiple metastases, with further complications of cerebral haemorrhage and oedema.
23. On 25 October 2012 the criminal proceedings were terminated as the commission of an offence had not been proven based on the evidence gathered. An appeal lodged by the applicant with the Office of the Prosecutor General was dismissed on 10 December 2012. On 28 January 2013 the Tallinn Court of Appeal dismissed a further appeal lodged by the applicant.
24. Following the termination of the criminal proceedings, the Office of the Prosecutor General dismissed complaints lodged by the applicant regarding the refusal to initiate additional criminal proceedings against the chief inspector of the Health Board’s supervisory department, against the experts of the Estonian Forensic Science Institute who had drawn up the forensic medical report during the original criminal proceedings (this refusal was later upheld by the Court of Appeal), against two prosecutors and the judge of the Court of Appeal. The Office of the Prosecutor General also dismissed an application lodged by the applicant to reopen the original criminal proceedings.
variables.forum: the European Court of Human Rights
variables.plaintiff_claim: The applicant asks the Court to find that Estonia violated Article 2 § 1 of the Convention (right to life) on the facts of this case.
variables.standard: Standard of review: the applicant must show an interference with a Convention right and that the State failed its Convention obligations -- the interference lacked a legal basis or a legitimate aim, or was not necessary in a democratic society (disproportionate), or the State breached a positive obligation. The State enjoys a margin of appreciation in weighing competing interests; where the domestic authorities gave relevant and sufficient reasons and the measure was proportionate, find no violation. Absent a demonstrated failure by the State, the default finding is no violation.
